title: Lesson 17. Arrays and methods
description: Indexes, length, push/pop, forEach, map, filter, find

learn.intro: Hi! Lesson 17 — **arrays and methods**. A shopping cart, an Instagram feed, a list of Telegram chats — they're all arrays. Let's go!

slides.text: One variable holds one value. But what if you need a list of 100 products? You won't create 100 variables! That's what **arrays** are for — a list in square brackets, elements separated by commas.
Every element has a number — an **index**:

If there's no such number, JavaScript doesn't complain — it just finds nothing: `fruits[10]` → `undefined`. You can replace an element: `fruits[0] = "kiwi";` — `const` forbids replacing the whole array, but you can change what's inside.
Indexing starts at ZERO. The first element is [0], not [1]. This is the most common beginner mistake.

check.prompt: What does fruits[1] print if fruits = ["apple", "banana", "pear"]?
check.explain: Counting starts at zero: [0] is apple, [1] is banana.

check.prompt: fruits[10] on a 3-element array throws an error.

slides.text: `.length` is how many elements the array has. It's written **without parentheses**: it's not an action, just a number.
There are 3 elements, but the last one's index is 2, because counting starts at zero. The last one is always fruits[fruits.length - 1].

check.prompt: An array has 5 elements. What is the index of the last one?

slides.text: `push` pushes to the end, like putting a product in a cart. `pop` takes out the last one. **Both change the array itself.**
Bonus: `pop()` also **returns** what it removed:

check.prompt: Which method adds an element to the end of an array?

slides.text: `forEach` means «for each». We give it a function, and it calls it for every element in turn. Arrow functions come in handy here!
`fruit` is a parameter: each round it holds the next fruit. You can name it anything. It's the same as `for...of` from lesson 15, just as an array method.
The second parameter is the **index**:

check.prompt: What goes into the second parameter of forEach((fruit, index) => …)?
check.explain: The second parameter is the index, starting at zero.

slides.text: `map` applies an action to every element and collects the results into a **NEW** array. The old one doesn't change. Prices with a 10% discount:
Proof of the difference: `forEach` returns nothing.
slides.code:
const x = prices.forEach((p) => p * 0.9);
console.log(x); // undefined

slides.text: forEach — does. map — does and gives back a new array.

check.prompt: After prices.map(...) the old prices array changes.
check.explain: map creates a new array, the old one stays the same.

slides.text: `filter` is like a sieve: it lets through only the elements for which the condition is **true**. It also returns a new array.
Remember `isEven` from the homework? It returns true or false — exactly what filter needs. You can even pass it by name: `numbers.filter(isEven)`.
`find` looks for the **first** element matching a condition and returns **the element itself**, not an array. If nothing is found — `undefined`.

Summary:
`forEach` — does something for each, returns **nothing**
`map` — changes each, **a new array of the same length**
`filter` — keeps the matches, **a new array** (may be shorter)
`find` — finds the first, **one element or undefined**

check.prompt: What does find return if nothing is found?
check.explain: find returns undefined, while filter would return [].
